initial_prompt: Explain quantum entanglement to me like I'm 10 years old.

messages.content: Explain quantum entanglement to me like I'm 10 years old.

Imagine you have two magic coins that are best friends.

When you flip them and separate them - even sending one to your grandma's house far away - something cool happens.

**When you look at your coin and it shows heads, your grandma's coin will ALWAYS show tails.** Every single time. It's like they're connected by an invisible string that works instantly, no matter how far apart they are.

The weird part? Before you look, neither coin has "decided" yet whether it's heads or tails. But the moment you peek at yours, the other one instantly "knows" what to be.

Scientists call this **entanglement**. Two tiny particles (way smaller than coins) can be linked like this in real life.

Einstein thought this was so strange he called it "spooky action at a distance" - because how does the other particle know what to do so fast?

It's like the particles are sharing a secret that even distance can't break.
